```{r helpers, include = FALSE}
}
fmt <- function(x, digits = 4) formatC(x, format = "f", digits = digits)

count_of <- function(tab, j) sum(tab$judgement == j)
```

## Model

Schnell and Ball (2016) monitor the rate of an adverse event of special
interest with blinded data: for each enrolled subject, the follow-up time
\(t_i\) and the number of events \(y_i\). With the unknown treatment
assignment \(a_i\) (1 for study drug),
\[
Y_i \mid a_i \sim \mathrm{Poisson}(\lambda_{a_i} t_i), \quad
a_i \sim \mathrm{Bernoulli}(k / (k + 1)), \quad
\lambda_c \sim \mathrm{Gamma}(\alpha_c, \beta_c), \quad
\lambda_d \sim \mathrm{Gamma}(\alpha_d, \beta_d),
\]
where \(k\) is the randomization ratio of study drug to control. The prior
of the control rate is informative (from historical control data), and the
prior of the study drug rate is weaker. A safety signal is raised when the
posterior probability that \(\lambda_d\) exceeds a critical rate is larger
than a threshold.

Summing over the assignment of each subject gives the likelihood
\[
\prod_i \left[ \frac{1}{k + 1} \lambda_c^{y_i} e^{-\lambda_c t_i} +
\frac{k}{k + 1} \lambda_d^{y_i} e^{-\lambda_d t_i} \right],
\]
so the posterior is two-dimensional. Schnell and Ball (2016) sample it by
Gibbs sampling; `exptime_post()` integrates it numerically. With event
indicators as `y` and the times at risk (up to the first event) as `t`, the
model is the exponential model for the time to the first event, which is how
`sim_oc()` uses it (model `"EXPTIME"`).

## Example

The priors of the case study of Schnell and Ball (2016): 339 events in
26,064 person-months of historical control data, and for the study drug the
same data discounted to one hundredth plus 4 events in 167 person-months
from a phase 2 study. The critical rate is 20% above the control rate
0.013, and the threshold is 0.62.

```{r data}
set.seed(1)
n <- 600
t <- runif(n, 2, 18)
drug <- rbinom(n, 1, 2 / 3)
y <- rpois(n, ifelse(drug == 1, 0.016, 0.011) * t)
c(subjects = n, events = sum(y), person_months = round(sum(t)))
```

```{r fit}
fit <- exptime_post(y, t, k = 2, prior_c = c(339, 26064),
                    prior_d = c(339 / 100 + 4, 26064 / 100 + 167),
                    rate0 = 1.2 * 0.013, cutoff = 0.62)
fit
```

The posterior probability of the rate ratio is also returned:

```{r probs}
fit$probs
```

Priors can be elicited from two quantiles with `elicit_prior()`; for
example, 50% sure that a rate is below 0.5 and 75% sure that it is below 2:

```{r elicit}
elicit_prior(c(0.5, 2), c(0.5, 0.75), "gamma")
```

## Numerical integration

```{r integration, include = FALSE}
v <- read_results("validation", "validate_methods_python.csv")
ve <- v[grepl("^PY_EXPTIME", v$id), ]
pe <- ve[grepl("prob", ve$id), ]
```

The posterior is integrated over \(\log \lambda_c\) by Gauss-Legendre
quadrature. For each of its nodes, the interval of \(\lambda_d\) that holds
the conditional posterior mass is located on the scale
\(z = \Phi^{-1}(F_d(\lambda_d))\), where \(F_d\) is the prior distribution
function of \(\lambda_d\), and the density is interpolated at Chebyshev
points in \(z\) or in \(F_d(\lambda_d)\), whichever represents it more
accurately. The first scale keeps the far tails of an informative prior,
which matters when the data put \(\lambda_d\) many prior standard
deviations above its prior mean; the second keeps a vague prior from
creating long tails. The posterior probability of a threshold that depends
on \(\lambda_c\) (such as the rate ratio) is obtained from the Chebyshev
series of each row. When the shape parameter of the prior of \(\lambda_c\)
is below 1, its density decreases slowly on the scale of
\(\log \lambda_c\) as \(\lambda_c \to 0\), where the blinded data do not
bound the posterior, and \(\Phi^{-1}(F_c(\lambda_c))\) with the prior
distribution function \(F_c\) of \(\lambda_c\) is used instead of
\(\log \lambda_c\). Compared with independent Python computations on dense
grids split exactly at the thresholds
(`inst/validation/validate_methods_python.R`, three data sets including one
with a study drug rate far in the upper tail of the prior of Schnell and
Ball, 2016, and a prior of \(\lambda_c\) with shape parameter 0.7), the
largest absolute difference of the `r nrow(pe)` posterior
probabilities is `r fmt_e(max(pe$abs_diff))`, and all `r nrow(ve)` compared
quantities are
`r if (all(ve$judgement == "PASS")) "PASS" else "not all PASS"`.

## Comparison with MCMC

```{r mcmc, include = FALSE}
j <- read_results("validation", "validate_jags_methods.csv")
je <- j[grepl("^J2_EXPTIME", j$id), ]
```

A JAGS model with the latent treatment assignments
(`inst/validation/validate_jags_methods.R`, 4 chains of 50,000 draws) gives
the following results for a data set of 60 subjects.

```{r mcmc-table, echo = FALSE}
knitr::kable(data.frame(quantity = je$quantity, MCMC = fmt(je$reference),
                        bssd = fmt(je$bssd), judgement = je$judgement),
             align = "lrrl")
```

## Reproduction of Schnell and Ball (2016)

```{r repro, include = FALSE}
r2 <- read_results("reproduce", "reproduce_Schnell2016.csv")
```

`inst/reproduce/reproduce_Schnell2016.R` generates the simulated case study
with the data generation of the authors' code and seed 1, and compares
Table 2 and the prior elicitation example: `r count_of(r2, "PASS")` PASS,
`r count_of(r2, "EXPLAINED")` EXPLAINED, `r count_of(r2, "FAIL")` FAIL and
`r count_of(r2, "INFO")` INFO. The posterior summaries in Table 2 are
Monte Carlo estimates of the authors' Gibbs sampler, whose Metropolis step
uses Poisson probabilities of the arm totals; bssd computes the posterior of
the subject-level model above. The reasons for the items that are not PASS
are in `inst/reproduce/results/SUMMARY.md`.

```{r author-code, echo = FALSE, results = "asis"}
fa <- res_file("validation", "schnell2016_author_code.csv")
if (nzchar(fa)) {
  a <- read.csv(fa, stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
  cat("The authors' code was run outside the package ",
      "(the code has no stated license): with seed 1 it reproduces the ",
      "published probabilities, and with 200,000 draws its sampler and a ",
      "sampler with the subject-level likelihood give the following ",
      "probabilities that the study drug rate exceeds 0.0156.\n\n", sep = "")
  print(knitr::kable(data.frame(
    month = a$interim, published = fmt(a$published_prob, 3),
    authors_code = fmt(a$author_prob, 3),
    authors_sampler = fmt(a$author_long_prob, 3),
    subject_level_sampler = fmt(a$subject_long_prob, 3),
    bssd = fmt(a$bssd_prob, 3)), align = "rrrrrr"))
}
```

```{r repro-table1, echo = FALSE, results = "asis"}
f1 <- res_file("reproduce", "reproduce_Schnell2016_table1.csv")
if (nzchar(f1)) {
  r1 <- read.csv(f1, stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
  cat("The simulation of Table 1 (control rate 0.0130, 1000 trials per ",
      "setting with the authors' seeds; ",
      "`inst/reproduce/reproduce_Schnell2016_simulation.R`) gives ",
      count_of(r1, "PASS"), " PASS, ", count_of(r1, "EXPLAINED"),
      " EXPLAINED and ", count_of(r1, "FAIL"), " FAIL items.\n", sep = "")
} else {
  cat("The simulation of Table 1 (`inst/reproduce/",
      "reproduce_Schnell2016_simulation.R`) has not been run for this ",
      "installation.\n", sep = "")
}
```
